finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token with the caller-supplied token using loose '==' (type juggling). A non-string or numeric-string token can match a stored token without being equal, which lets an attacker reset a victim's password. Verdict: PLAUSIBLE, conditional on token format and caller input types.
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password_loose (reset.php:2). It is caller-supplied and not validated in this file. The caller is not in the repo, so the attacker-controlled channel (HTTP form, JSON body) is unverified.
finding.sink: Password overwrite: UPDATE users SET pw = ... (reset.php:5-6).

trace.note: $token enters as an untyped parameter with no is_string check.
Stored token is fetched by email via $db->quote; the email is not an injection vector here.

Loose '==' comparison. If $token is boolean true, any non-empty stored token matches. If $token is null (parameter absent), an empty stored token matches. If both stored and supplied values are numeric strings, PHP 8 compares them numerically, so '0e123' == '0e456' is true.
On match, the password is replaced with password_hash($new) for the email, with no further check.

finding.guards_checked: Email is escaped with $db->quote (line 3 and 6), so no SQL injection was found, assuming a PDO connection. The $row truthiness check only requires that a row exists for the email. There is no strict type check on $token, no hash_equals, no empty-token rejection, and no expiry or single-use check. Exploitability depends on the caller passing raw JSON booleans or on numeric-looking stored tokens; neither is visible in this repo.
finding.repro: Case A (JSON caller): stored token 'abc123...' for victim; POST {"email":"victim@x","token":true,"new":"pw"} to a route that forwards $token unchanged. true == 'abc123' is true, so the password is overwritten. Case B (numeric token): stored token '0e462097431906509019562988736854'; submit token '0e1' (both numeric strings equal 0), so the comparison matches.

verdict.guard_found: None inside reset_password_loose. reset.php:4 uses loose == with no is_string/hash_equals/empty-token check, and the only check is row existence (reset.php:4). The sibling reset_password at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals with (string) cast, but reset_password_loose does not call it.
verdict.reason: The trace matches reset.php:2-6: the loose comparison at reset.php:4 is a real type-juggling flaw with no guard in the function, but reset_password_loose has no caller in the repo (Glob shows only reset.php), so whether an attacker can supply a boolean or crafted token over HTTP, and whether any stored token is numeric-looking, cannot be decided from this code.

finding.claim: reset_password's hash_equals() accepts an empty supplied token when the stored token is NULL or empty, because PHP coerces null to '' for internal functions. This allows a password reset with no valid token. Verdict: PLAUSIBLE, conditional on the resets table allowing NULL or empty tokens. The same empty-value issue also affects the loose check on line 4.
finding.source: $token, supplied by the caller (reset.php:12). The cast (string)$token on line 14 turns null or an absent parameter into ''. An attacker can send an empty token.
finding.sink: Password overwrite: UPDATE users SET pw = ... (reset.php:15-16).

trace.note: $token is untyped, so null or missing values are accepted.
Stored token fetched by email. If the row's token column is SQL NULL, PDO returns null for $row['token'].
hash_equals(null, '') coerces null to '' and returns true, since hash_equals(string, string) takes internal-function scalar coercion. The $row check does not reject an empty stored token.
Password is overwritten for the email.

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals is a constant-time comparison, which is the correct primitive, but it does not reject empty or null inputs. There is no check for an empty stored token or an empty supplied token. Whether NULL or '' tokens can occur depends on the schema and the token-generation code, which are not in the repo. On PHP 8.1+ the coercion emits a deprecation notice but still proceeds.
finding.repro: If resets has a row for victim@x with token NULL (or ''), POST {"email":"victim@x","token":"","new":"pw"}. Stored token coerces to '', supplied token is '', hash_equals returns true, and the password is overwritten. Line 4 (reset_password_loose) has the same outcome, since null == '' and '' == '' are true.

verdict.guard_found: none. reset.php:14 uses hash_equals with no check for empty or null values. Line 13 does not reject an empty stored token, and there is no check on $token before line 14. reset.php:4 (reset_password_loose) uses a loose == with no guard. The repo contains no caller, no HTTP layer, and no schema or token-generation code.
verdict.reason: The mechanism is real: reset.php:14 passes $row['token'] (null when the column is NULL) to hash_equals, which coerces null to '' under PHP's non-strict internal-function coercion, so an empty supplied token matches (and reset.php:4 has the same null == '' issue). However, trace step reset.php:12 is misdescribed: a missing argument throws ArgumentCountError rather than being accepted, so trace_ok is false. Whether any row can hold a NULL or '' token, and whether an anonymous caller can reach reset_password at all, depends on the schema and the caller, which are not in the repo, so the verdict is UNVERIFIABLE.

finding.claim: Reset tokens are never consumed or expired by the code in this file. A valid token can be reused indefinitely to reset the password. This is a logic flaw in both reset functions. Severity depends on whether the caller or the schema enforces expiry or invalidation, which I could not verify.
finding.source: A valid reset token for the victim's email. The attacker obtains it from a previously sent reset email, a log, a leak, or any other earlier exposure. This precondition is not in the repo.
finding.sink: Password overwrite: UPDATE users SET pw = ... (reset.php:15-16 for reset_password; reset.php:5-6 for reset_password_loose).

trace.note: reset_password_loose SELECT fetches only the token column. No created_at or expiry column is read.
reset_password SELECT fetches only the token column. No created_at or expiry column is read.
reset_password_loose returns true after updating the password. No DELETE or UPDATE of the resets row occurs anywhere in this file.
reset_password returns true after updating the password. The resets row remains, so the same token still matches.

finding.guards_checked: Searched the whole file: no DELETE or UPDATE on resets, no expiry comparison, and no used flag. fetch() returns a single row with no ORDER BY, so when several reset rows exist for an email, the one checked is arbitrary. This means an old outstanding token may still be valid after a newer one is issued. Expiry and invalidation may exist elsewhere (schema trigger, caller, cron job), which would reduce severity.

verdict.guard_found: none in reset.php. Token comparison at reset.php:4 (==) and reset.php:14 (hash_equals) is the only check. Neither consumes nor expires the row. No DELETE/UPDATE on resets and no expiry column is read (reset.php:3, 13). The repo contains only reset.php (Glob), so no schema, trigger, cron job, or caller is present to add a control.
verdict.reason: All trace lines match the file: reset.php:3 and :13 select only token, reset.php:7 and :17 return true after the UPDATE with no resets-row deletion, so the same token still passes the check at reset.php:4 and :14. The attacker must already hold a valid token (a bearer secret from an earlier reset email or log), so impact is reuse after a legitimate reset rather than unauthenticated takeover, and severity stays uncertain until an external schema trigger or caller is checked.
